standard_prerequisites.name: Equinumerosity
standard_prerequisites.statement: A is equinumerous with B when there is a bijection f from A to B.
standard_prerequisites.use: This is the definition unfolded at each of the three steps (source lines 1019-1031).

standard_prerequisites.name: Closure properties of bijections
standard_prerequisites.statement: The identity map of a set is a bijection; the inverse of a bijection is a bijection; the composite of two composable bijections is a bijection.
standard_prerequisites.use: The three clauses of the proof use exactly one of these three facts each (source lines 1019-1020, 1024-1026, 1029-1031).

core_obligations: Reflexivity: exhibit the identity map of A and observe that it is a bijection from A to A, so A is equinumerous with A (source lines 1019-1021).
Symmetry: from a bijection f from A to B, form its inverse, note that the inverse is a bijection from B to A, and conclude B is equinumerous with A (source lines 1023-1026).
Transitivity: from bijections f from A to B and g from B to C, form the composite of f with g, note that it is a bijection from A to C, and conclude A is equinumerous with C (source lines 1028-1031).

proof_roadmap.step: Reflexivity via the identity map of A.
Symmetry via the inverse of the witnessing bijection.
Transitivity via the composite of the two witnessing bijections.

difficulty_reason: The counted unit is the author's own proposition equinumerosityisequi at source lines 1011-1013: equinumerosity, defined as the existence of a bijection, is an equivalence relation. The proof at source lines 1015-1032 is short but is not a single appeal to the definition: it must produce three different bijections, and each of the three clauses asks for a different construction on the witnessing maps. Reflexivity needs the identity map to be recognised as a bijection, symmetry needs the inverse of a bijection to be a bijection (and to be written with the right domain and codomain), and transitivity needs the composite of two bijections to be a bijection. The argument therefore rests on three closure properties of bijections that the statement does not mention, and on carrying the witnessing functions through the definition at each step. No result outside the retained text is used.

compared.difference: prop:enum-bij (statement 926-930, proof 932 onward) counts the rigid reformulation of a surjective enumeration as a bijection onto a finite or positive-integer domain; our candidate counts the equivalence-relation property of equinumerosity as a relation between arbitrary sets. The two proofs share no step.
thm:nonenum-pownat counts Cantor's theorem that the power set of the naturals is not enumerable, with a diagonal argument; our candidate is an order-theoretic property of the equinumerosity relation.
